conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a perinatal mental-health clinician, and my job is simply to listen and help you feel supported as you settle into new motherhood. Over the next few minutes we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—to check in on how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically during the past week. It’s not a test of your parenting; it’s just a quick way to see if you might benefit from extra support right now. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me you’re in immediate danger, and we can pause or stop at any time. I’ll ask 10 short questions; you can answer however feels most comfortable, and I’ll jot down your score so we can talk about next steps together. Ready to start?

First question: Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Yeah, I’ve still been able to laugh—mostly when my husband makes silly faces at the baby or when the dog tries to “help” during tummy-time. It’s not quite as effortless as before I was pregnant, but funny moments still get a genuine chuckle out of me.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yes, most of the time I still find things funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things
Yes, I still look forward to little things—like my morning coffee once the baby settles, or taking her for a walk in the stroller. They’re small moments, but they feel good.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Not really. I mean, if she spits up right after I’ve changed her outfit, I might think, “Should I have waited longer after feeding?”—but I don’t beat myself up. I figure babies are just messy and I’m learning.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little bit, yeah. Sometimes I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly wonder if her breathing sounds funny or if she’s gaining enough weight, even though the pediatrician just said she’s doing great. It’s not constant, but it pops up out of nowhere a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
No, I haven’t felt scared or panicky. A bit on-edge when she fusses and I can’t figure out why, but it’s not that same sudden rush of fear.
Things have been getting on top of me

Sometimes, yeah—like when she cluster-feeds and I can’t get to the dishes or answer a text. For a minute it feels as if the to-do list is towering, but once she nods off I can usually reset and chip away at it.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, I’ve been sleeping pretty well—well, as well as anyone whose nights are broken up every three hours. Once she’s back down I can usually drift off again without much trouble.
I have felt sad or miserable
Not really. I have my tired moments, but I wouldn’t call them sad or miserable—more like “ready-for-a-nap” than down or blue.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Hardly at all. Maybe once when I was extra tired and she wouldn’t latch, but it was brief—more frustration than sadness.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. That hasn’t crossed my mind.

You're navigating the familiar swirl of new parenthood-smiling at your husband's silly faces, savoring that first cup of coffee, and pushing through the occasional wave of worry when tiny concerns pop up about your baby's breathing or the never-ending to-do list. Despite some fleeting anxious thoughts and moments when chores feel like they're piling up, you're still finding joy in small routines and have not felt persistently low, panicky, or hopeless.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 6, Risk Level: Depression not likely (concerns include <sym>Patient describes spontaneous worries about baby's breathing and weight several times daily, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges feeling overwhelmed "sometimes" and describes specific moments of inability to manage tasks, matching the "Yes, sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual" option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scoring places you well below the threshold for probable <med>postpartum depression</med> (scores ≥12-13). You endorsed mild, situation-specific <sym>anxiety</sym> several times daily and brief sensations of being overwhelmed, but you denied core mood symptoms such as persistent sadness, anhedonia, guilt, sleep disruption unrelated to infant care, panic attacks, or self-harm thoughts. These findings do not meet <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> which requires ≥5 symptoms (including depressed mood or loss of interest) for two weeks accompanied by clinically significant distress or impairment. Your description is consistent with common post-birth adjustment rather than a depressive episode. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Keep doing what helps-sharing laughs, getting outside for stroller walks, and accepting that dishes can wait
2. Use quick grounding tools (slow breathing, 5-4-3-2-1 sensory check) when worries surface
3. Aim for one longer stretch of rest: trade night shifts with your partner or nap when baby sleeps
4. Re-screen with EPDS at the two-month visit or sooner if mood drops or worries intensify
5. Stay connected-text a friend, join a new-mum group, or schedule short coffee meet-ups
6. If anxiety becomes daily and distressing, or low mood persists >2 weeks, contact your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> for further evaluation
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 6: Screening note – Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) responses reviewed 6 wk PP

Symptoms endorsed
• Intermittent, situation-linked anxiety (Q4) – 2–3× daily intrusive “what-if” worries about infant health; no panic attacks
• Mild, episodic sense of being overwhelmed during cluster-feeding periods (Q6); resolves once infant settles

Symptoms denied
• Persistent low mood, anhedonia, guilt, self-blame, crying spells, sleep-onset problems unrelated to infant care, panic, self-harm ideation

Pattern
Transient, context-dependent distress without pervasive mood or cognitive symptoms typical of major PPD; no safety concerns identified.
